newsitem.title: CHINA: Fees, taxes curbing China housing market growth.
newsitem.headline: Fees, taxes curbing China housing market growth.

text.p: Huge land use fees, taxes and public utility costs are holding back development of China's housing market and leaving vast amounts of living space unused, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.

China had 50.3 million sq m (538 million sq ft) of housing sitting empty but property developers had been unable to sell it because high fees and taxes had put it out of the reach of middle and low income families, the newspaper said.
The average cost of a two-room urban home was about 300,000 yuan ($36,000), equal to a middle-income worker's salary for 30 years, the newspaper said.
"The lofty price is a result of massive fees," it said.
Land rental fees and taxes were responsible for up to 60 percent of the cost of housing, it said.
About 400,000 families had less than 4.0 sq m (43 sq ft) of living space, it said.
The slump in housing purchases had hit the property sector hard, with more than half of real estate firms registering a decline in profits, it said.
Industry officials had urged more efforts to cut prices and bring housing within the reach of middle and low income families, it said.

"They suggest prices should be streamlined, omitting long-term land rent and fees for public facilities while reducing taxes," the newspaper said, adding that such measures could slash housing prices by up to 30 percent.
Tough terms for mortgages had also discouraged residents from making housing purchases, it said.
Monthly interest rates for 15-year loans were about 1.0 percent, meaning home buyers had to pay thousands of yuan in interest each month, it said.
The Ministry of Construction was drafting policies to try to revive the residential housing market and encourage individuals to buy homes, it said.

China's four largest state-run commercial banks -- the Construction Bank of China, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, the Agricultural Bank of China and the Bank of China -- earlier this month relaxed limits on personal mortgages to try to encourage people to buy housing.
China has announced plans to build 1.2 billion sq m (12.9 billion sq ft) of urban housing by the year 2000.
